summary: Cuban-born singer and bandleader whose Afro-Cubans, built with music director Mario Bauzá, fused Cuban rhythm with swing-band horns. The band laid the groundwork for Latin jazz and later salsa.
know: The Afro-Cubans formed in New York in 1940 with his brother-in-law Mario Bauzá as music director.
Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie both recorded with the band in the late 1940s.
He won a Grammy in 1983 for Machito and His Salsa Big Band.
keyAlbums: Machito and His Salsa Big Band

influencedBy.why: Bauzá shaped the band's horn charts on the voicings of the big swing orchestras, Ellington's above all.
Bauzá came to the Afro-Cubans straight from Chick Webb's band and carried its drive into the new group.
Bauzá's stint in Calloway's orchestra gave the Afro-Cubans their model of a polished, show-ready big band.
The band's montunos and conjunto rhythms draw on the Cuban son that Arsenio was expanding in the same years.

influenced.why: Puente played in Machito's band early on and built his own orchestra on the same Afro-Cuban big-band model.
Through Bauzá and the band, Gillespie absorbed the Cuban rhythm that fed his Afro-Cuban bebop and later shared albums with Machito.
Parker soloed over the Afro-Cubans on the Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite sessions, an early meeting of bebop and Cuban rhythm.
Palmieri grew up on the Palladium-era sound that Machito helped define and kept its big-band harmony in salsa.
The Fania stars inherited the brassy New York Latin orchestra format that Machito pioneered.

cousins.why: A swinging big band built around riffs and a locked-in rhythm section.
A large horn band that turned dance rhythm into long, layered workouts.

summary: Cuban pianist and bandleader who became the 'King of Mambo' after moving to Mexico City. His blaring trumpets, grunts and tight riffs turned mambo into a worldwide dance craze in the 1950s.
know: He built his career in Mexico City after leaving Cuba in the late 1940s.
Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White topped the US charts for 10 weeks in 1955.
His trademark shouted 'Ugh!' cues his horn section in many recordings.
songs: Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White

influencedBy.why: The López brothers' late-1930s danzón 'Mambo' introduced the syncopated section Prado blew up into a full style.
Arsenio's riff-based montunos are a widely cited root of the mambo Prado popularized.
Moré sang with Prado's orchestra in Mexico City, and their records together defined the early mambo sound.

influenced.why: Puente's New York mambo orchestra rode the international craze that Prado's hits created.

cousins.why: A big band that turned a dance style into a pop chart phenomenon.
Shouted cues and stabbing horns used to drive a dance floor.

summary: Pianist and bandleader whose trombone-heavy La Perfecta changed the sound of New York Latin music in the 1960s. He pushed salsa toward jazz harmony and long, open-ended jams.
know: La Perfecta replaced the usual trumpets with two trombones and a flute.
The Sun of Latin Music won the first Grammy for Best Latin Recording in 1975.
He often named Thelonious Monk and McCoy Tyner as models for his piano voicings.

influencedBy.why: Palmieri came up in the Palladium scene Puente led, learning the big-band mambo idiom.
Machito's fusion of jazz harmony and Cuban rhythm set the template Palmieri pushed further.
He credited Monk's angular voicings for the dissonant chords in his piano montunos.
His hard-driving montunos follow the son conjunto approach Arsenio created.
The modal, extended solos on his 1970s records echo the Coltrane quartet, especially McCoy Tyner's piano.

influenced.why: La Perfecta's trombone frontline is widely seen as the blueprint for Colón's own trombone-led bands.
The long descarga workouts at Fania concerts follow the jam-heavy style Palmieri championed.

cousins.why: A pianist-bandleader who built hard-swinging grooves from Latin and gospel roots.
A bandleader who stretched dance grooves into long, jazz-inflected jams.

summary: Trombonist and bandleader from the Bronx who signed to Fania as a teenager and helped define the raw New York salsa sound. His partnerships with Héctor Lavoe and Rubén Blades produced some of the genre's most celebrated records.
know: He released his debut El Malo at about 17.
His band's two-trombone front line gave his records a rough, brassy edge.
Siembra, made with Rubén Blades, became one of the best-selling salsa albums ever.

influencedBy.why: Colón took the trombone-led sound of Palmieri's La Perfecta and made it harsher and more street-level.
He grew up on the New York mambo orchestras Puente led.
His bands drew on the son montuno structure and conjunto feel Arsenio established.

influenced.why: Colón made Lavoe his lead singer, and their run of Fania albums launched Lavoe's career.
Colón co-led Siembra and other albums with Blades, giving his socially minded songs a major platform.
As a core member he helped shape the group's sound and repertoire.
Anthony's salsa draws on the Colón and Lavoe catalog that defined the New York style.

cousins.why: Dance music that carried pointed social commentary.
A horn-driven bandleader who wrote about city life and politics.

summary: Puerto Rican singer known as 'El Cantante' whose nasal, quick-witted voice fronted Willie Colón's band and later his own. He became one of salsa's most beloved stars and its definitive improvising sonero.
know: He moved from Ponce, Puerto Rico, to New York at 17.
His recordings with Willie Colón began with El Malo in 1967.
Rubén Blades wrote El Cantante for him, and it became his signature song.

influencedBy.why: Colón made him his singer and shaped his early career and sound.
Blades wrote El Cantante for him, giving Lavoe his defining song.
His improvised soneos follow the Cuban sonero tradition that Moré personified.

influenced.why: Anthony has called Lavoe a major influence and played him in the 2006 film El Cantante.
His lead vocals, such as Mi Gente at Yankee Stadium, became Fania All-Stars landmarks.

cousins.why: A golden voice whose phrasing defined a genre's lead singer.
A singer who sounded best improvising over a live band.

summary: Panamanian singer, songwriter and actor who brought story-driven, socially observant lyrics to salsa. His albums with Willie Colón and later with Seis del Solar widened what salsa songs could be about.
know: He joined Fania in New York in the 1970s after starting out in Panama.
Siembra, his 1978 album with Willie Colón, is one of salsa's best-selling records.

influencedBy.why: Colón was his main creative partner, co-leading the albums that made him a star.

cousins.why: A songwriter who tells detailed stories about working people.
Pointed social observation set to a groove.

summary: The house supergroup of Fania Records, assembled by Johnny Pacheco and Jerry Masucci, that gathered the label's top bandleaders and singers on one stage. Their concerts and films spread New York salsa worldwide.

influencedBy.why: Their open jam format follows the Cuban descargas Cachao led in the 1950s.
The all-star big-band lineup carries on Machito's model of New York Latin orchestras.
Puente's Palladium-era showmanship set the standard the Fania stars aimed at.

Anthony's generation learned salsa from the Fania catalog and concerts.

Top session players backing a whole label's worth of hits.

summary: New York singer of Puerto Rican descent who began in freestyle and house before becoming the top-selling tropical salsa artist of his era. He also crossed into English-language pop in the late 1990s.

His dramatic, lyric-driven salsa owes a debt to Blades's songwriting.
He draws on the Colón and Lavoe catalog that defined New York salsa.

cousins.why: A big romantic voice who made ballads feel like events.
A singer who moved between club music and grown-up balladry.

summary: An ensemble of veteran Cuban musicians gathered in Havana by Juan de Marcos González and Ry Cooder. Their 1997 album and Wim Wenders's film revived global interest in prewar Cuban son and bolero.

The group's boleros follow the guitar-trio romantic style Los Panchos made popular.

cousins.why: Veteran musicians brought to world audiences with help from Ry Cooder.
An older master whose late recordings revived an overlooked style.

summary: Cuban-born singer who fronted Miami Sound Machine and became the first major Latin pop crossover star of the 1980s. Working with Emilio Estefan, she mixed conga rhythms with American dance-pop and later returned to Cuban roots on Mi Tierra.
know: She joined Emilio Estefan's Miami Latin Boys in 1975, and the group became Miami Sound Machine.
Conga in 1985 was a breakthrough single for Latin rhythm on US pop radio.
Mi Tierra in 1993 was a Spanish-language album of traditional Cuban styles that won a Grammy.

influencedBy.why: Cruz was the leading Cuban exile voice whose music she grew up hearing in Miami.
Mi Tierra revisits the classic Cuban son and orchestra sound of Moré's era.
Her Spanish ballads and boleros follow the romantic style Los Panchos popularized.

Her crossover proved a Latin artist could top US pop charts, the path Martin followed.
Selena's mix of Latin roots and dance-pop followed the lane Estefan opened.

cousins.why: 1980s dance-pop built to fill a club and a stadium.
A bright 1980s pop voice with a big personality.

summary: East Los Angeles band that moves between Mexican folk, R&B, blues and rock, often on the same album. They are best known for their 1987 La Bamba remake and the experimental 1992 album Kiko.
know: They spent years playing traditional Mexican music before turning to rock in the early 1980s.

summary: Argentine bandoneón player and composer who reinvented tango by bringing in jazz harmony and classical form. Tango traditionalists resisted him at first, but his nuevo tango became the style's best-known modern voice.

summary: Singer, songwriter and film star who made tango a sung art form and became its first international star. His recordings and films in the 1920s and 1930s set the standard for tango vocalists.

summary: Argentine singer known as 'La Negra' whose deep voice made her the leading interpreter of Latin American folk and nueva canción. She sang songs by many writers and became a symbol of Argentine popular music.

influencedBy.why: She recorded his songs and performed with him, linking folk to Argentine rock in the 1980s.

summary: Chilean singer, songwriter and theater director who became a leading figure in nueva canción. His plain, direct songs about rural workers and ordinary life made him one of Latin America's most honored songwriters.

cousins.why: A songwriter whose plain songs spoke for working people.

summary: Bahian singer, guitarist and songwriter who co-founded Tropicália with Caetano Veloso, mixing Brazilian forms with rock and psychedelia. He later folded reggae, funk and northeastern styles into a long, influential career.

His closest collaborator, with whom he built the Tropicália movement.
Sgt. Pepper-era Beatles shaped Tropicália's mix of studio experiment and pop.
Hendrix's electric guitar fed Gil's late-1960s rock turn.

influenced.why: Os Mutantes backed him on Domingo no Parque at the 1967 festival, a starting point for Tropicália.

summary: Rio singer and guitarist whose percussive guitar style blended samba with rock, soul and funk. Songs like Mas Que Nada and País Tropical became Brazilian standards and reached audiences worldwide.

summary: Singer and songwriter from Minas Gerais whose soaring voice and modal, folk-tinged songs anchored the Clube da Esquina collective. His work drew in jazz musicians from Wayne Shorter to Herbie Hancock.

summary: Singer from southern Brazil widely regarded as the country's greatest vocalist of her era. She launched the careers of songwriters such as Milton Nascimento and Belchior by recording their songs.

summary: Rio singer who came out of funk carioca to become Brazil's biggest global pop star, singing in Portuguese, Spanish and English. In 2022 Envolver made her the first Brazilian solo artist to top Spotify's global chart.
